config.title: Python security

intro.title: Python security
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple password strength checker to learn the basics of Python security. You'll use Python's built-in `re` module to apply regular expressions for validating password patterns, such as requiring uppercase letters, digits, and special characters. The core programming concept involves writing functions to process user input and implementing conditional logic to evaluate security criteria. By the end, you'll understand how to create a basic tool that helps enforce secure password practices in Python applications.
intro.usecase: Python security practices are essential in real-world applications like user authentication systems in web platforms, where developers must securely handle passwords and session tokens. These principles appear in financial dashboards that protect sensitive transaction data through proper input validation and encryption. Security measures are also critical in API endpoints for e-commerce sites, ensuring payment information isn't exposed to injection attacks. Every Python developer implements these patterns when building secure forms, admin panels, or data processing tools that handle user information.

objectives: Implement input validation to sanitize user data
Configure secure password hashing using bcrypt
Construct parameterized SQL queries to prevent injection attacks
Initialize environment variables for sensitive configuration
Apply proper exception handling to avoid information leakage
Manipulate file permissions to restrict unauthorized access
Integrate HTTPS enforcement in web application configurations

steps.instruction: Define a function named generate_secure_token that returns a cryptographically secure random token using the secrets module.

steps.title: Add the program entry point
steps.instruction: Add the conditional block `if __name__ == '__main__':` at the bottom of your script to call the main() function when the program runs directly.
steps.hint: In Python, `__name__ == '__main__'` checks if the script is being run as the main program (not imported as a module). Place this condition at the end of your file and indent the call to main() inside it.
